extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria on choosing and handling the 'pictorial' (panoramic) versus 'dramatic' (scenic/enacted) methods in novel-writing — when to summarize and when to enact, how to handle narrator presence, character-typicality, and preparation of climactic scenes. Useful for writers shaping long novels and students analysing novel technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic / pictorial method
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel may present its material as a continuous flow of leisurely, contemplative reminiscence; the narrative is steeped in a suffusion of general tone and the sensation of place rather than a series of strictly staged scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retrospective, panoramic treatment to produce an impression of manners, society, and a broad 'world' rather than a tight plot. Let scene melt into scene, allow the backward-ranging thought to linger, and gather a long train of experience into a unified impression. This is right for subjects that require an expansive survey rather than dramatic point-to-point action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity by typicality rather than intricate plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The unity of a panoramic novel often 'depends in truth upon one fact only, the fact that all his throng of men and women are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world from which they are taken' rather than on tightly interwoven plot links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a chronicle of manners or a social panorama, light or slight links between characters are often sufficient; the book's cohesion comes from collective representation of a time/place rather than from a single central plot or entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic enactment required for climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: When an impression culminates in a decisive catastrophe or turning-point, that moment must be placed 'immediately before us' as present action; narration alone will not have the force required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve direct, scenic presentation (enactment) for climactic scenes so the reader can 'see' the event for themselves. Convert retrospective account into an immediate scene where necessary to give answers proper emphasis and warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excessive authorial mediation in crucial scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author persists in intervening at moments that should be enacted, the force of the scene is impaired; characters must sometimes be left to 'take the matter into their own hands' and act without the narrator's continual interposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-explain or summarise when the material calls for present action. Allow characters autonomy in pivotal scenes; step back from the narrative voice to let the drama function without overt authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare big scenes in advance — avoid belated theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to prepare a major dramatizable scene in advance forces the writer into 'devices of some crudity' to make the climax conclusive; sudden theatrical heightening looks artificial if not properly anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure earlier chapters supply sufficient character rendering and situational preparation so that when the scene is enacted its effect is natural rather than forced. Use earlier glimpses and incidents to build toward the climax rather than relying on late intensification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional episodes vs mere decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes that appear within the panorama should be 'functional' to the book's purpose — they should contribute to the impression or hinge of a character's career — not merely decorative digressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inserting lively interludes or episodes, make sure they advance the reader's sense of character, social texture, or the novel's thematic arc rather than merely repeating prior material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of detail: foreshortening and fusion of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In panoramic narration, small incidents often 'spring up' in memory to illustrate the general effect; a hint, a moment, a glance suffices and is brushed past without elaborate staging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise, telling particulars — brief glimpses and swift impressions — to enrich the panorama. Avoid over-particularizing every moment; a few vivid touches will reinforce the broad impression without slowing the retrospective flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong, picturesquely typical characters in a crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: In a novel that aims to portray a society, characters should be 'strongly, picturesquely typical' so that each in their different way 'can add to the force of its effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling a large cast, focus on making each major figure an emblematic presence of the milieu. Their cumulative typicality contributes to the overall portrait and supplies unity in the absence of a tightly interlocked plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between picture and drama (reader relation to writer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture (pictorial method) implies the reader faces the story-teller and attends to the author's mind; drama implies the reader watches the story itself with the author effaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose your dominant method deliberately: pictorial narration foregrounds the author's presence and retrospective authority; dramatic treatment seeks to efface the author and let events present themselves. Be consistent so the reader's relation to the text is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of an insistent, unaccounted narrator in pictorial method
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial panorama often makes the creative mind (the omniscient narrator) conspicuous; if that seeing eye is not authenticated within the book, the novel may have 'an inconclusive look' and invite questioning of its authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid undermining the fiction's validity, either dramatize the seeing eye (include the point-of-view within the book) or otherwise account for the narrator's knowledge. Make the narrator's presence verifiable so the book does not feel unfinished or externally supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to 'dramatize the seeing eye'
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelists may adopt means to make the narrator's point-of-view objective, i.e., to 'authenticate his story—to dramatize the seeing eye.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed the narrator's perspective into the fiction (for example by aligning with a character's consciousness or supplying on-stage verification) so that the reader can accept the source of knowledge; this counters the weakness where omniscience seems unaccountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of scope: use picture for breadth, drama for intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial method enables coverage of vast social regions and many facts; drama yields intensity but is limited in scope. As plot thickens, 'narration gives place to enactment' where emphasis is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use panoramic narration to sweep over broad social or temporal territory; switch to dramatic enactment for moments that require intensity and immediacy. Be mindful of each method's limitations and blend them where appropriate to serve both breadth and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and placement of telling moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain brief, well-chosen moments (e.g., Becky at the piano, a single glimpse of a character) can lift an episode into dramatic effect even within a largely pictorial work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select single, crystalline incidents to dramatize or to supply ocular proof of a narrator's claim. Even half-page scenes can produce dramatic advancement if placed at the right moment and used sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraying time as 'stored up' versus movement
rubrics_metrics.description: To give the sensation of time as tranquillity rather than continuous movement, the novelist may 'roam to and fro' in chronology and shift focus so time 'is stored up in the description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 'time-pictures' (moments where time deepens rather than moves), use leisurely play with chronology, delays, and returns to create layers of time. This method is effective for portraying atmospheres and long-embedded states rather than action-driven progress.
